error_modes.label: Final approach airspeed control after FAF

texts.0: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the computed final approach airspeed, did not stabilize speed after the FAF and made no corrective throttle input as the trend developed. Airspeed diverged past plus 15 and minus 10 knots from the computed value and continued to drift while the descent was flown. IP had to direct the power change to recover the approach speed before the MAP.
texts.1: SP, due to a late and coarse throttle response to a decaying descent profile, did not hold the computed final approach airspeed after the FAF. Airspeed reached the plus 15 and minus 10 knot limit and was returned toward the computed value only after verbal prompting from IP. The correction was applied with a delay that left the speed unsettled into the MDA segment.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction made before the descent rate was established, allowed the computed final approach airspeed to erode after the FAF. Airspeed reached the band between plus 10 and plus 15 knots fast and minus 5 and minus 10 knots slow, but SP recognized the trend on the airspeed indicator and restored the computed value with a timely throttle correction and no intervention.
texts.3: SP set power against the computed final approach airspeed immediately after the FAF and held it through the descent to MDA. Airspeed stayed inside plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed value, with small anticipatory throttle corrections applied as configuration and descent rate changed. Speed control did not degrade course or altitude tracking.
texts.4: SP established the computed final approach airspeed at the FAF on the first power setting and flew the entire final segment with negligible speed excursions. Throttle inputs were small, anticipatory and matched to configuration and wind changes, so the airspeed indicator remained essentially steady from FAF to MAP. Speed discipline left full attention available for course and altitude control.
texts.marginal: SP kept the computed final approach airspeed within standards but worked the throttle in repeated large corrections, so speed oscillated close to the fast side of tolerance through the final segment. The trend was toward late recognition of the decaying descent profile rather than anticipation of it. SP is expected to set power against the computed airspeed at the FAF and refine it with small inputs on subsequent approaches.

texts.0: SP, due to chasing raw course deviation with uncoordinated heading changes instead of establishing and holding a wind correction angle, did not maintain the published final approach course. Course displacement exceeded 8 degrees from the inbound radial and continued to increase toward the MAP. IP had to take corrective action to return the aircraft to the published course.
texts.1: SP, due to an unrecognized crosswind on the inbound radial, did not apply a wind correction angle and allowed the aircraft to drift steadily off the published course. Displacement reached the 8 degree limit and was corrected only after verbal instruction from IP, with the aircraft still recentering as MDA was approached. The correction was applied late and required more than one heading change to settle.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially insufficient wind correction angle after course intercept, allowed displacement from the inbound radial to grow into the band between 5 and 8 degrees. SP recognized the deviation on the course indicator, applied a measured heading correction, and reestablished the published course before the MDA segment without intervention.
texts.3: SP intercepted the published final approach course and held it inside 5 degrees throughout the inbound segment. A wind correction angle was established early and adjusted in small increments, so course deviation stayed centered rather than oscillating. Tracking was maintained through the descent without degrading airspeed or altitude control.
texts.4: SP intercepted the inbound radial cleanly and held the published course with negligible displacement to the MAP. The wind correction angle was identified within the first part of the final segment and required only minor refinement thereafter, keeping the course indicator effectively centered. Tracking precision was maintained while airspeed and altitude were simultaneously flown to tolerance.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the published final approach course within standards but tracked it with a repeating series of small overshoots either side of the radial rather than a settled wind correction angle. The trend was toward correcting deviation after it appeared instead of holding a computed drift correction. SP is expected to establish the wind correction angle at intercept and hold heading to keep the course indicator centered.

texts.0: SP, due to an unarrested descent rate approaching the published minimum descent altitude, did not level off at MDA and did not respect the zero tolerance below it. The aircraft went below MDA, or remained more than 200 feet above it while the MAP passed, without corrective action by SP. IP had to intervene on the controls to restore the published minimum descent altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power addition during the level off, did not capture the published minimum descent altitude at the planned point. Altitude settled at the 200 foot limit above MDA and was corrected toward the published value only after verbal prompting from IP. The delay consumed a significant part of the segment available before the MAP.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent rate not reduced early enough before level off, overshot the level altitude and stabilized between 100 and 200 feet above the published MDA. SP recognized the deviation on the altimeter, corrected with a timely descent to the published minimum descent altitude, and at no point descended below it or required intervention.
texts.3: SP anticipated the level off, reduced descent rate in time and captured the published minimum descent altitude within 100 feet above it with no descent below MDA. Altitude was then held steady to the MAP while course and airspeed were maintained. Power and pitch were coordinated so the level off did not disturb the approach speed.
texts.4: SP levelled off precisely at the published minimum descent altitude with negligible overshoot and no descent below it. Altitude was held essentially constant from level off to the MAP, with pitch and power coordinated so airspeed and course were unaffected by the transition. Altimeter control required no visible correction during the level segment.
texts.marginal: SP held the published minimum descent altitude within standards but captured it with a shallow oscillation and stayed consistently toward the upper part of the allowed band. The trend was toward starting the level off late and recovering the altitude rather than arriving at MDA already stabilized. SP is expected to anticipate the level off point and settle on the published minimum descent altitude with a single correction.

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete listening watch while setting up the approach, did not comply with an ATC instruction affecting the approach clearance. The assigned heading, altitude or clearance limit was not flown as issued and no readback was made that would have exposed the discrepancy. IP had to intervene with ATC and on the controls to restore compliance.
texts.1: SP, due to a transmission received while the navigation aid was being retuned, did not act on an ATC instruction until the deviation was already established. Compliance was achieved only after IP prompted verbally, and the aircraft was at the edge of the cleared parameter when the correction started. Readback was incomplete and did not include the assigned altitude.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed readback of an ATC instruction issued during the intercept, was late in starting the assigned turn or altitude change. SP detected the omission without prompting, read back the clearance correctly and complied within the approach parameters, so the deviation remained bounded and self-corrected.
texts.3: SP maintained an accurate listening watch throughout the approach, read back ATC instructions correctly and complied with each clearance promptly. Assigned headings, altitudes and clearance limits were flown as issued while the approach parameters were maintained. Radio work did not interrupt aircraft control or approach setup.
texts.4: SP handled all ATC instructions on the approach with correct, concise readbacks and immediate compliance, without any prompting. Clearances were integrated into the approach plan as they were received, so no assigned parameter was ever in question. Radio discipline was maintained with no measurable effect on flight parameter control.
texts.marginal: SP complied with all ATC instructions but consistently needed a repeat of the clearance before reading it back, and compliance began later than the traffic situation warranted. The trend was toward processing the instruction after the flying task rather than integrating the two. SP is expected to maintain a continuous listening watch and read back clearances on first transmission.

texts.0: SP, due to reading the approach plate without cross-checking the step-down fixes against DME or radial position, violated a published routing or altitude restriction as depicted in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals. The aircraft descended below a published minimum segment altitude or flew outside the depicted track. IP had to intervene to restore the published profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an unverified fix identification during the intermediate segment, initiated descent before the applicable step-down fix and reached the published segment minimum at the limit of tolerance. The profile was corrected only after IP pointed out the restriction, and the aircraft remained low on profile for part of the segment. The published routing itself was maintained.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent started slightly early against the depicted step-down profile, allowed the aircraft to approach the published segment minimum before the fix. SP cross-checked DME and the approach plate, recognized the discrepancy and arrested the descent in time, so no published routing or altitude restriction was violated and no intervention was required.
texts.3: SP flew the depicted routing and honored every published altitude restriction from the initial segment to the MAP. Step-down fixes were identified by DME or radial before descent was initiated, and segment minima were respected throughout. The approach plate was used actively rather than from memory.
texts.4: SP flew the published routing and every segment altitude restriction with negligible deviation and no reference error. Each step-down fix was positively identified before descent, and the resulting profile matched the depicted procedure throughout. Plate management was orderly enough that no restriction required a late check.
texts.marginal: SP respected all published routing and altitude restrictions but identified several step-down fixes only just before the descent point, leaving no margin for a misread. The trend was toward late confirmation of the depicted profile rather than early planning of it. SP is expected to brief and confirm the step-down fixes before the segment begins.

error_modes.label: Approach setup, navaid tuning and identification

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the approach phase, did not complete the approach setup before the intercept and did not tune and identify the VOR or TACAN facility for the final approach course. The approach was flown on an unverified or incorrect navigation source, contrary to the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manual. IP had to intervene to correct the navigation setup.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that left the approach setup until after the descent had begun, did not tune, identify and set the final approach course in time for a stabilized intercept. The setup was completed only after IP prompted, and the intercept was flown at the outer limit of the course tolerance while the equipment was still being configured. No item was left unset at the FAF.
texts.2: SP, due to a compressed task sequence on the transition to the approach, was late in identifying the VOR or TACAN facility and in setting the final approach course. SP detected the omission during the approach check, completed the setup before the intercept without prompting, and the approach was flown on a verified navigation source throughout.
texts.3: SP completed the approach setup in good time, tuned and positively identified the VOR or TACAN facility and set the final approach course before the intercept. The sequence followed the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manual with no omitted item. Setup work was spread so that aircraft control was never interrupted.
texts.4: SP planned and executed the approach setup ahead of the aircraft, with the facility tuned and identified and all navigation and cockpit items configured well before the intercept. The sequence matched the standardized procedures exactly and left spare capacity for the ATC and flying tasks. No setup item required rework at any stage of the approach.
texts.marginal: SP completed the full approach setup and identified the facility correctly, but the work was compressed into the last part of the transition and left little margin before the intercept. The trend was toward reactive rather than planned task sequencing under increasing approach workload. SP is expected to complete the tune, identify and course set earlier so the intercept is flown from a settled cockpit.

texts.0: SP, due to an unmonitored station passage or DME reference, did not execute the required actions at the FAF and did not initiate the descent at the correct point. Time, configuration or descent initiation were wrong to the extent that the profile could not reach MDA before the MAP without an excessive descent rate. IP had to intervene to reestablish the published descent profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an ambiguous station passage indication that was not cross-checked against DME, delayed the FAF actions and started the descent late. Descent initiation was at the limit of what the segment allowed, and the required rate had to be increased after IP prompted the correction. Timing and configuration items at the FAF were completed out of the standard sequence.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on course centering at station passage, was late by a short interval in starting time and initiating the descent at the FAF. SP recognized the omission promptly, completed the FAF actions and adjusted descent rate within normal limits so that MDA was reached in good time without intervention.
texts.3: SP identified the FAF positively, started time where required and initiated the descent at the correct point with the aircraft correctly configured. The descent rate selected was appropriate to groundspeed and the remaining distance to MDA. FAF actions were executed in the standardized sequence without omission.
texts.4: SP executed the FAF sequence precisely at station passage, with time started, configuration set and descent initiated in one coordinated flow. The descent rate was computed to groundspeed so that MDA was reached with an unhurried margin before the MAP. No FAF item was late or repeated.
texts.marginal: SP completed all FAF actions and started the descent within standards, but the sequence was executed item by item after station passage rather than as a prepared flow, leaving the descent slightly late. The trend was toward reacting to the fix instead of anticipating it. SP is expected to have the FAF actions prepared and to initiate the descent immediately at station passage.

error_modes.label: Instrument cross-check during the final segment

texts.0: SP, due to a scan that fixated on the course indicator to the exclusion of the other instruments, did not cross-check attitude, altitude and airspeed during the final segment. Deviations in the unmonitored parameters developed unnoticed and were still increasing when they exceeded approach tolerances. IP had to intervene to reestablish the flight parameters.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan narrowed onto the parameter being corrected, did not cross-check the remaining instruments and let a second parameter drift to the limit of tolerance while the first was being fixed. The drift was recognized only after IP called it out, and recovery of both parameters was still in progress at MDA. The scan remained sequential rather than integrated for the rest of the segment.
texts.2: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check while retuning and rechecking the navigation display, allowed a secondary parameter to move into the outer part of the approach tolerance band. SP restored a full instrument scan without prompting, detected the deviation on the next sweep and corrected it in time, keeping all parameters within limits.
texts.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of attitude, course, altitude and airspeed throughout the final segment. Deviations were detected while still small and corrected with single measured inputs, so no parameter approached its tolerance. The scan absorbed the radio and configuration tasks without breaking.
texts.4: SP flew the final segment on a fully integrated instrument cross-check, detecting trends before they became deviations. All approach parameters were held with negligible excursion while ATC calls and cockpit tasks were handled in stride. The scan rate never narrowed onto a single instrument, even during the level off at MDA.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the approach parameters within standards but the cross-check visibly slowed each time a correction was made, so the other instruments were sampled less often during those periods. The trend was toward a scan that narrows under a single-parameter correction. SP is expected to keep the full cross-check running while correcting, so trends are detected before deviations develop.

error_modes.label: MAP recognition and missed approach decision

texts.0: SP, due to continuation bias in maintaining the approach past the point at which the required conditions were not met, did not execute the missed approach at the MAP and did not respect the published minimum descent altitude. The aircraft continued beyond the MAP or descended below MDA without the required references. IP had to take control to initiate the missed approach.
texts.1: SP, due to persisting with the approach while looking for the required references, did not initiate the missed approach at the MAP and reached the limit of the published minimum without a decision. The go-around was started only after IP directed it, and the initial climb and heading were flown late relative to the published missed approach procedure. No descent below MDA occurred.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late recognition of the MAP against time and DME, delayed the missed approach decision by a short interval. SP identified the MAP without prompting, initiated the published missed approach procedure with correct power, pitch and configuration, and the delay produced no deviation beyond approach tolerances.
texts.3: SP identified the MAP by time or DME, made the decision without hesitation and initiated the published missed approach procedure immediately. Power, pitch, configuration and the published climb heading were applied in the standardized sequence. The minimum descent altitude was respected throughout the decision.
texts.4: SP arrived at the MAP with the decision already made against the briefed criteria and executed the published missed approach procedure without hesitation. The transition to climb was flown with the correct power, pitch and configuration sequence and an accurate climb heading, with negligible altitude loss or heading excursion. The published minimum was respected at every stage.
texts.marginal: SP executed the missed approach at the MAP within standards but the decision was visibly made at the fix rather than briefed in advance, producing a short pause before power was applied. The trend was toward extending the approach in the hope of acquiring the required references. SP is expected to state the decision criteria before the approach and act on them at the MAP without pause.

error_modes.label: Heading changes larger than 5 degrees on final - overcontrolling the course

texts.0: SP chased the CDI with heading changes far larger than the 5 degrees the technique allows, turning well outside the area beneath the heading bug on every correction. Each input overshot the final approach course and reversed the needle, so the aircraft never settled on the inbound radial. Displacement exceeded 10 degrees from the published course, past the code 1 limit, and IP took the controls and set a single heading to stop the oscillation.
texts.1: SP corrected course deviations with heading changes of 15 to 20 degrees instead of limiting them to 5 degrees under the heading bug, which produced a steady overcorrection either side of the inbound radial. The swings reached about 8 degrees off course, at the code 1 limit, and only IP's repeated calls to halve the corrections and fly a fixed heading brought the tracking back to standard.
texts.2: SP made the first two corrections with heading changes near 10 degrees, wider than the area beneath the heading bug, and overshot the final approach course. Displacement reached roughly 6 to 7 degrees, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP recognised the overcontrol, reduced the corrections to 5 degrees and re-centred the CDI without prompting.
texts.3: SP corrected deviations from the inbound radial with heading changes held to 5 degrees, keeping every correction within the width of the heading bug. Course displacement stayed inside 4 degrees, within the code 3 tolerance, and the needle showed no reversal through the final segment.
texts.4: SP set specific headings for each deviation and kept the changes well under 5 degrees, so the corrections stopped the drift without any overshoot. Course displacement never exceeded about 1 degree and the CDI remained effectively centred from the FAF to the MAP.
texts.marginal: SP kept the heading corrections just under the 5 degrees the technique allows, but applied them in the same repeating sequence, so the aircraft crossed the inbound radial each time rather than settling on it. Displacement stayed inside the code 3 tolerance, near 4 to 5 degrees at the peaks, with a clear oscillating trend that grew as the approach continued. SP is expected to reduce the correction once the needle starts to move and hold the resulting heading.

error_modes.label: Wind corrected heading not computed and heading bug not marked for the final

texts.0: SP did not determine the wind from the GPS, did not apply the 60 to 1 rule to convert the crosswind component into drift, and left the heading bug on the last assigned heading instead of the wind corrected final heading. Flying raw course with no drift allowance, the aircraft was blown steadily downwind of the inbound radial and the displacement passed 10 degrees, beyond the code 1 limit, before IP intervened with a heading to regain the course.
texts.1: SP omitted the drift calculation and marked no wind corrected heading on the bug, so the crosswind on final was met with a series of guessed corrections. The aircraft settled downwind of the inbound radial at about 8 degrees, the code 1 limit, and the tracking was restored only after IP called out the track error and dictated the correction to be flown.
texts.2: SP set the heading bug to the published final approach course without the drift correction, having compared aircraft track to heading only after the FAF. The drift opened the displacement to roughly 6 degrees from the inbound radial, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP derived the correction from the GPS track and re-established the course on his own initiative.
texts.3: SP computed drift from the known wind with the 60 to 1 rule and marked the wind corrected heading on the bug before the FAF. Course displacement remained inside 4 degrees, within the code 3 tolerance, with only small refinements needed on the inbound leg.
texts.4: SP determined the wind with the GPS, converted the crosswind component into drift and bugged the wind corrected heading before configuring, then refined it by comparing track to heading. Displacement from the inbound radial never exceeded about 1 degree and the correction required no visible change after the FAF.
texts.marginal: SP calculated the drift and bugged a wind corrected heading, but used the reported surface wind rather than the GPS wind at approach altitude, so the correction was slightly undersized. Course displacement stayed within the code 3 tolerance, near 4 degrees at worst, with a consistent drift to the downwind side that had to be trimmed out twice. SP is expected to cross-check GPS track against heading after the FAF and refine the bugged heading accordingly.

error_modes.label: Configuring later than 2-3 NM prior to the FAF - airspeed and trim not stabilized

texts.0: SP started configuring at the FAF instead of 2 to 3 NM before it, so gear, flaps TO and the Before-Landing Checklist were still in progress while the descent had already begun. Airspeed and trim were never stabilized at the 110 KIAS approach speed and the aircraft accelerated past 130 KIAS in the descent, beyond the code 1 tolerance for computed final approach airspeed. IP intervened with power and trim to recover the approach speed and had the checklist completed.
texts.1: SP delayed configuration until about 1 NM prior to the FAF, leaving no room to stabilize airspeed and trim before descending. With the aircraft still out of trim at descent initiation, airspeed reached about 125 KIAS, at the code 1 limit for computed final approach airspeed, and it was recovered only after IP called for power and trim corrections.
texts.2: SP configured just inside 2 NM prior to the FAF, so the aircraft was configured but not yet trimmed hands-off when the descent started. Airspeed reached roughly 122 KIAS, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP set the descent torque, retrimmed and returned to 110 KIAS shortly after the FAF without prompting.
texts.3: SP configured 2 to 3 NM prior to the FAF, allowing airspeed and trim to stabilize before the descent, and completed the Before-Landing Checklist before reaching the fix. Airspeed after the FAF stayed within the code 3 tolerance of the computed final approach speed, inside 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow.
texts.4: SP configured with gear down and flaps TO 3 NM prior to the FAF, completed the Before-Landing Checklist and had the aircraft trimmed at 110 KIAS well before the descent. Airspeed after the FAF varied by no more than 2 to 3 knots from the computed final approach speed.
texts.marginal: SP configured close to the 2 NM limit and completed the Before-Landing Checklist just at the fix, so the trim was still being adjusted as the descent started. Airspeed after the FAF remained within the code 3 tolerance, peaking near 9 knots fast, but required continuous attention to hold. SP is expected to configure at 3 NM prior to the FAF so airspeed and trim are settled before descent.

error_modes.label: Large power corrections on final instead of small torque adjustments

texts.0: SP corrected small airspeed errors with large power movements rather than the small torque adjustments the technique calls for around the 16 percent non-precision final setting. Each coarse power change drove the airspeed through the target and forced an opposite correction, so the aircraft was never stabilized on the computed final approach speed. Excursions exceeded 20 knots fast and 15 knots slow, beyond the code 1 tolerance, and IP took over the power lever to stabilize the approach.
texts.1: SP made repeated large power corrections on the final segment when only a few percent of torque was required, producing airspeed swings that reached about 15 knots fast and 10 knots slow, at the code 1 limits for computed final approach airspeed. The oscillation stopped only after IP directed SP to set the descent torque value and leave it alone.
texts.2: SP reacted to an airspeed error with a large power reduction instead of a small torque adjustment, and the airspeed swung about 12 knots off the computed final approach speed, between the code 3 and code 1 limits. SP recognised the overcontrol, restored the descent torque setting and had the airspeed back within tolerance well before the MDA.
texts.3: SP held the descent torque setting on final and used only small power adjustments for the airspeed errors that appeared. Airspeed stayed within the code 3 tolerance of the computed final approach speed throughout the segment, inside 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow.
texts.4: SP set the non-precision descent torque at the FAF and corrected with adjustments of a couple of percent only, avoiding any large power change. Airspeed remained within 2 to 3 knots of the computed final approach speed from the FAF to the MDA.
texts.marginal: SP used mostly small torque adjustments but reached for a larger power change twice when the airspeed decayed, which each time required an opposite correction. Airspeed stayed inside the code 3 tolerance, close to 9 knots fast at the peaks, with a widening pattern of corrections toward the MDA. SP is expected to reserve large power corrections for excessively high or low airspeed only.

error_modes.label: Pitch changes larger than 2 degrees for descent corrections on the final segment

texts.0: SP corrected the descent with pitch changes far larger than the 2 degrees, roughly 400 feet per minute on the VSI, that the technique allows, so the vertical path oscillated instead of converging. Chasing the VSI in this way, SP descended through the MDA before the aircraft was in a position to land, which is outside the tolerance of both codes since no deviation below the MDA is permitted. IP intervened to arrest the descent and climb back to the minimum altitude.
texts.1: SP made pitch corrections of 4 to 5 degrees during the descent, each producing vertical speed changes well beyond 400 feet per minute, and levelled off high after the overcontrol. The aircraft settled about 200 feet above the MDA, at the code 1 limit, and descended to the minimum only after IP prompted for the pitch and power required to arrest the error.
texts.2: SP used a pitch change of about 3 degrees to correct the descent rate and overshot the level-off, ending roughly 150 feet above the MDA, between the code 3 and code 1 limits. SP then reduced the corrections to 2 degrees, re-established the descent and reached the MDA in time to continue the approach without prompting.
texts.3: SP limited pitch corrections to 2 degrees, about 400 feet per minute on the VSI, and the level-off at the minimum was controlled. Altitude settled within 100 feet above the MDA, inside the code 3 tolerance, with no descent below the minimum.
texts.4: SP corrected the descent with pitch changes of a degree or less and anticipated the lag of the VSI, so the level-off required no reversal. The aircraft stabilized within about 20 feet above the MDA and held it to the MAP.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pitch corrections at about 2 degrees but applied them late, so each level-off at the minimum was completed with a small overshoot. Altitude stayed within the code 3 tolerance, close to 100 feet above the MDA, with a tendency to level high and then need a second descent. SP is expected to lead the level-off and correct with pitch changes no larger than 2 degrees.

error_modes.label: Descent gradient not calculated for step-down fix restrictions inside the FAF

texts.0: SP did not calculate the descent gradients required for the step-down fix altitude restrictions inside the FAF, so the descent was flown at a rate picked at random rather than one derived from the distance and the altitude to lose. The aircraft arrived at the step-down fix well above the published restriction and then descended at a rate far beyond the 1.000 feet per minute non-precision value, ending below the MDA, which is outside the tolerance of both codes. IP intervened to stop the descent and re-establish the minimum altitude.
texts.1: SP flew the segment inside the FAF without computing the descent gradient for the step-down fix, and the rate used was insufficient for the altitude to be lost over the remaining distance. The aircraft was still about 200 feet above the MDA at the point where the approach should have been stabilized, at the code 1 limit, and reached the minimum only after IP called the deviation and the rate required.
texts.2: SP computed the gradient for the FAF to MDA segment but not for the step-down fix inside it, so the initial descent rate was too low and had to be increased. The aircraft was roughly 150 feet high on the profile, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP recalculated the rate against DME and regained the profile without prompting.
texts.3: SP calculated the descent gradients for the step-down fix and for the final segment before the approach and flew the corresponding rates against DME. Altitude at the restriction and at the minimum stayed within 100 feet above the published value, inside the code 3 tolerance, with no descent below any minimum.
texts.4: SP derived the descent gradient for every altitude restriction inside the FAF during the approach setup and cross-checked altitude against DME at each mile. The profile was flown within a few tens of feet of the calculated altitudes and the MDA was reached with the aircraft stabilized.
texts.marginal: SP calculated the descent gradients but did not convert them into a target rate of descent, so the rate was adjusted by trial against DME on each mile. Altitude remained within the code 3 tolerance, close to 100 feet high at the step-down fix, with a consistent tendency to arrive high and then increase the rate. SP is expected to convert the gradient into feet per minute before the FAF and fly it directly.

error_modes.label: Configuration and approach airspeed not adjusted for crosswind or gusty conditions

texts.0: With gusty winds reported on the final approach course, SP configured with the standard flap setting and made no increase to the approach airspeed, which the technique requires when crosswinds or gusts are present. Each gust then produced a large airspeed excursion that SP tried to chase with power, and the computed final approach speed was exceeded by more than 15 knots fast and lost by more than 10 knots slow, beyond the code 1 tolerance. IP intervened to set a gust corrected airspeed and stabilize the approach.
texts.1: SP flew the final in gusty conditions at the plain computed approach speed, without the airspeed increase called for by the technique, so every gust translated straight into an airspeed error. The excursions reached about 10 knots slow and 15 knots fast, at the code 1 limits, and were contained only after IP directed a gust correction and a fixed torque setting.
texts.2: SP recognised the gusty conditions late and added the airspeed increase only after the FAF, leaving the first part of the final segment flown at the plain approach speed. Airspeed dropped roughly 7 knots below the computed value in one gust, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP set the corrected airspeed and stabilized the descent on his own.
texts.3: SP configured with the appropriate flap setting and increased the approach airspeed for the reported crosswind and gusts before the FAF. Airspeed on final stayed within the code 3 tolerance of the computed value despite the gusts, inside 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow.
texts.4: SP briefed the gust factor, configured accordingly and flew a gust corrected approach airspeed held with small torque adjustments. Airspeed excursions from the corrected value stayed within about 3 knots through the whole final segment.
texts.marginal: SP applied an airspeed increase for the gusty conditions but sized it to the steady wind rather than to the gust spread, so the margin was thin on the strongest gusts. Airspeed stayed within the code 3 tolerance, dipping close to 5 knots below the computed value twice, with the trend worsening as the aircraft descended toward the MDA. SP is expected to base the correction on the gust factor and adjust the flap setting to match.
